'''Sun Wenguang''' ({{lang-zh|t=孫文廣|s=孙文广}}; born August 26, 1934) was an activist and vocal critic of the Chinese government. He was a professor of Physics at [[Shandong University]] in Jinan from 1982 until 1994 when he retired.

== Early life ==
Sun Wenguang was born in [[Rongcheng City]] on August 26, 1934. His father was a naval officer of the National Government. Sun joined the Navy in his early years. {{citation needed|date=May 2020}}

== Career ==
Sun was a professor of Physics at [[Shandong University]] in Jinan from 1982 until 1994 when he retired.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.voanews.com/a/who-is-chinese-professor-wenguang-sun/4511975.html|title=Sun Wenguang - China Action|website=Cuawg.wikidot.com|access-date=2018-08-03}}</ref>

== Activism ==
Sun has a history of criticizing the Chinese government, being one of the original signatories of [[Charter 08]] and has been harassed for relations with critics of Communist China.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://via.hypothes.is/https://www.nytimes.com/2009/04/08/world/asia/08china.html|title=China Rights Activist Beaten in Cemetery|last=LaFraniere|first=Sharon|access-date=2018-08-03}}</ref>

On April 5, 2009, Sun and a university student left to go to a local cemetery called Heroes’ Mountain (Yingxiong Shan; 英雄山) on a holiday to honor the dead. He was to visit the grave of [[Zhao Ziyang]], a former [[Premier of the People's Republic of China|Chinese Premier]] and [[Communist Party of China|Communist Party]] [[General Secretary of the Communist Party of China|general secretary]] who died in 2005. When Sun entered the cemetery in Jinan, four or five men attacked him and beat him severely. He was admitted shortly after to Jinan hospital with three broken ribs and injuries to his spine, head, back, arms and legs. Later in 2010, Sun's passport application was rejected shortly before the [[Nobel Peace Prize]] ceremony for [[Liu Xiaobo]].{{citation needed|date=August 2018}}

On August 1, 2018, Sun was giving an interview with [[Voice of America]] in which he expressed opinions about [[Communist Party of China|Chinese Communist Party]] [[General Secretary of the Communist Party of China|general secretary]] [[Xi Jinping]] and government expenditures outside China when the interview was ended abruptly after Chinese security forces entered his house and seized him. Sun is reported to be locked in currently and two VOA journalists Feng Yibing and Allen Ai were seized for several hours after trying to reach Sun in August 2018.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.businessinsider.com/sun-wenguang-china-critic-claims-locked-in-home-2018-8|title=A renegade Chinese professor who was forced off-air while criticizing the government says he was locked in his apartment and told to make up a story that he left town }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/08/02/world/asia/china-sun-wenguang-voa.html|title=A Chinese Activist Was Challenging Xi on Live TV. The Police Came to Stop Him.|date=2018-08-02|work=New York Times|access-date=2018-08-03}}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine|url=https://time.com/5357116/wenguang-sun-missing/|title=Chinese Academic Reportedly Missing After Critical Interview|magazine=Time|access-date=2018-08-03}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/worldviews/wp/2018/08/03/here-they-come-again-chinese-police-arrest-dissident-professor-during-on-air-interview/|title='Here they come again': Chinese police arrest dissident professor during on-air interview|newspaper=Washington Post|access-date=2018-08-03}}</ref>

In 2022, it was reported that Sun may have died in 2021, at the age of 87. However, the relevant Chinese authorities refused to confirm the validity of these reports.<ref>{{cite news |title=孙文广被人间蒸发4年 知情者称已离世而当局仍封锁消息 |url=https://www.voachinese.com/a/dissident-sun-wenguang-passed-away-in-secret-police-custody-sources-say/6710313.html |access-date=25 September 2024 |publisher=Voa |date=21 August 2022}}</ref>

== Writing ==
His books, published in Hong Kong, include:
* ''Against the Wind for 33 Years: Dictatorship after 1977 versus Constitutional Democracy''
* ''Essays from Within and Without of Prison''
* ''Calling for Freedom''
* ''A Country in a Century of Trouble: From Mao Zedong to Jiang Zemin''
* ''Essays on Chinese Central Government and CCP from Prison''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.hrw.org/news/2012/12/20/writers-honored-commitment-free-expression|title=Writers Honored for Commitment to Free Expression|date=20 December 2012|website=Human Rights Watch|access-date=5 August 2018}}</ref>
